input.reasoning_summary:
After investigating potential challenges to the initial verdict, the SUPPORTED label remains appropriate.

H1 (Explicit mention of cannibalization): The retrieved evidence (E7-E9) only provides definitions of metrics like paid clicks and cost-per-click. There is no evidence in the Q3 2026 10-Q explicitly mentioning generative AI cannibalizing or negatively impacting search advertising. NO_RELEVANT_EVIDENCE.

H2 (Growth from pricing vs. volume): Evidence E14 shows monetization metrics for Q2 2026 (not Q3 2026, so period mismatch), but it demonstrates that paid clicks grew 13% while cost-per-click grew only 3-4%. This pattern suggests growth was driven primarily by volume (clicks) rather than just pricing increases, which would refute the concern that pricing masked volume declines. While this is Q2 data, the pattern is consistent with healthy volume growth. CHALLENGE_REFUTED.

H3 (AI risks to monetization): Evidence E15 discusses potential future effects of AI incorporation on monetization in forward-looking language ("we may monetize differently," "could affect"). This is from the 2025 10-K and is forward-looking, not a statement about observed Q3 2026 results. It does not provide evidence that AI features actually reduced ad clicks or monetization in Q3 2026. NO_RELEVANT_EVIDENCE.

The original supporting evidence remains valid: Google Search & other revenues grew substantially ($6.8 billion or 12% year-over-year in Q3 2026), driven by increases in search queries, advertiser spending growth, and ad format improvements. No evidence contradicts this or shows cannibalization effects. The claim that Q3 2026 results show generative AI is not cannibalizing search advertising is SUPPORTED by the strong revenue growth and positive drivers disclosed in the filing.
